CausalChain: Fasting -> Energy Stress in HCC cells -> Upregulation of miR-199a-5p (+ additional miRNAs) -> Downregulation of HK2 and PKM2 (validated via CRISPR screens) -> Reduced Aerobic Glycolysis (Warburg effect) -> Shift to Oxidative Phosphorylation -> Lower Lactate Production -> Reduced Lactate-Mediated Immune Evasion -> Enhanced Sorafenib Sensitivity
Hypothesis: Under fasting conditions, the resulting energy stress in hepatocellular carcinoma cells induces an increase in miR-199a-5p expression (and likely a coordinated set of other miRNAs), which directly target and downregulate the glycolytic enzymes HK2 and PKM2. This downregulation shifts cellular metabolism away from the Warburg effect toward increased reliance on oxidative phosphorylation. The consequent reduction in lactate production diminishes lactate-mediated immunosuppression, ultimately resulting in enhanced sensitivity to sorafenib in HCC. Modern technologies such as CRISPR-based transcriptomic screening, single-cell metabolomics, and advanced imaging will be employed to rigorously validate each step of this pathway, paving the way for integrative metabolic and immunotherapeutic strategies to overcome drug resistance in liver cancer.
Abstract: This study hypothesizes that fasting-induced energy stress in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells triggers a cellular response marked by the upregulation of miR-199a-5p—and potentially a network of complementary microRNAs—leading to the direct suppression of key glycolytic regulators, hexokinase-2 (HK2) and pyruvate kinase isozyme M2 (PKM2). Utilizing advanced omics approaches including CRISPR interference screening, single-cell transcriptomics, and metabolomic profiling, we propose that this miRNA-mediated downregulation shifts tumor metabolism from a predominantly glycolytic (Warburg effect) phenotype to one that preferentially utilizes oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). This metabolic reprogramming reduces lactate production, thereby alleviating lactate-mediated immunosuppression within the tumor microenvironment and ultimately restoring sensitivity to sorafenib in drug-resistant HCC models. The proposed model not only deepens our mechanistic understanding of fasting-induced metabolic changes in HCC but also highlights novel therapeutic strategies that exploit metabolic vulnerabilities in concert with existing treatments.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that fasting upregulates miR-199a-5p leading to the downregulation of HK2 and PKM2, with a subsequent metabolic shift that reduces lactate-mediated immune evasion and reverses sorafenib resistance in HCC. The revised hypothesis retains this core causal chain but explicitly integrates contemporary technologies and a broader systems biology approach. Specifically, it emphasizes the use of CRISPR screens and single-cell omics to validate the direct targeting of HK2 and PKM2 by miR-199a-5p, considers the role of additional miRNAs, and provides a more detailed mechanistic basis for the fasting-induced energy stress. These modifications enhance the practical implementability and scientific rigor of the hypothesis while still reflecting the original step-wise causal reasoning.
